title: Adding in the garden: tens, ones and regrouping
objectives: I can say how many tens and ones are in a two-digit number.
I can add two two-digit numbers by adding the tens and then the ones.
I can regroup 10 ones as 1 ten when the ones add up to 10 or more.
I can add a two-digit number to a three-digit number.
introduction: Imagine you have a vegie patch and today is planting day. You have a tray with 47 tomato seedlings and your neighbour hands you another tray with 36 lettuce seedlings. Before you can decide how many holes to dig, you need to know how many seedlings there are altogether. Counting them one at a time would take ages, and you might lose your place! Today you will learn a quick, reliable way to add numbers like these in your head and on paper, the same way gardeners and shopkeepers do.

sections.heading: Tens and ones: how numbers are built
sections.body: Every two-digit number is made of tens and ones. Think of beans packed into little cups, with exactly 10 beans in each full cup. The number 47 means 4 full cups of ten and 7 loose beans left over: 4 tens and 7 ones, which is 40 + 7. The number 36 is 3 full cups and 6 loose beans: 3 tens and 6 ones, or 30 + 6. The digit on the left tells you how many tens, and the digit on the right tells you how many ones. This is called place value, and it is the secret behind adding quickly. When we know that 47 is really 40 and 7, we can pull numbers apart and put them back together without losing anything. Try it: how many tens and ones are in 52? (5 tens and 2 ones, so 50 + 2.)

visual.caption: 47 is 4 tens (the long rods) and 7 ones (the small cubes).

sections.heading: Adding tens and ones separately
sections.body: Here is the first adding strategy. To add 24 + 35, split both numbers into tens and ones. 24 is 20 + 4 and 35 is 30 + 5. Now add the tens together: 20 + 30 = 50. Then add the ones together: 4 + 5 = 9. Finally put the two answers back together: 50 + 9 = 59. So 24 + 35 = 59. This works because adding is just collecting groups: we collected all the tens into one pile and all the ones into another pile, then joined the piles. Notice we always add the tens and ones separately first, and only join them at the very end. This strategy is called partitioning, which means splitting numbers into parts. It is a great way to check your thinking before you write anything down.

sections.heading: What if the ones add up to 10 or more? Regrouping
sections.body: Sometimes the loose beans make more than a full cup! Let's add 47 + 36. Split the numbers: 47 is 40 + 7 and 36 is 30 + 6. Add the tens: 40 + 30 = 70. Add the ones: 7 + 6 = 13. But 13 ones is more than 10, so we can fill a cup: 13 ones is 1 ten and 3 ones. This is called regrouping (some people say 'trading' or 'carrying'). We trade 10 loose ones for 1 more ten. Now we have 70 + 10 + 3, which is 80 + 3 = 83. So 47 + 36 = 83. Whenever your ones total 10 or more, stop and ask: how many full tens can I make, and how many ones are left over? Then add the new ten to the tens you already have.

sections.heading: Writing it down: the column method
sections.body: Once you understand regrouping, you can write the same idea in columns, which is quicker. Write the bigger digits lined up: tens under tens and ones under ones. For 47 + 36, start with the ones column, because that is where regrouping happens. 7 + 6 = 13. Write the 3 in the ones column of the answer and carry the 1 ten by writing a small 1 above the tens column. Now add the tens column: 4 + 3 + the 1 you carried = 8. Write 8 in the tens column. The answer is 83, the same as before. The small 1 is not magic; it is the cup of ten you made from 13 loose beans. Always start with the ones and work to the left. Lining up the digits neatly is the most important habit for getting columns right.

sections.heading: Bigger numbers: adding to a three-digit number
sections.body: The same method works for bigger numbers. Let's add 138 + 45. The number 138 has 1 hundred, 3 tens and 8 ones. The number 45 has 4 tens and 5 ones. Keep the hundred to one side because nothing is being added to it. Add the tens: 30 + 40 = 70. Add the ones: 8 + 5 = 13, which is 1 ten and 3 ones. Now collect everything: 100 + 70 + 10 + 3. That is 100 + 80 + 3 = 183. So 138 + 45 = 183. In columns you would start at the ones again: 8 + 5 = 13, write 3 and carry 1; then 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 tens; the hundred comes down unchanged. The steps never change, no matter how big the numbers get: ones first, regroup if you reach 10, then tens, then hundreds.

worked_examples.title: No regrouping needed
worked_examples.problem: A gardener plants 24 carrots and 35 radishes. How many vegetables did she plant?
steps: Split into tens and ones: 24 = 20 + 4 and 35 = 30 + 5.

worked_examples.title: Regrouping the ones
worked_examples.problem: There are 47 tomato seedlings and 36 lettuce seedlings in the trays. How many seedlings are there altogether?
steps: Split into tens and ones: 47 = 40 + 7 and 36 = 30 + 6.
13 ones is more than 10, so regroup: 13 = 1 ten + 3 ones.

worked_examples.title: A three-digit number plus a two-digit number
worked_examples.problem: A sunflower patch has 138 seeds already sown. Then 45 more seeds are sown. How many seeds are in the patch?
steps: Add the ones: 8 + 5 = 13, which is 1 ten and 3 ones.
worked_examples.answer: There are 183 seeds in the patch.

visual.caption: After regrouping, 27 + 18 makes 4 tens and 5 ones.

guided_practice.prompt: Mia plants 32 tomato seedlings and 25 lettuce seedlings. How many seedlings did she plant?
guided_practice.hint: Split both numbers into tens and ones. Add the tens, then the ones.

guided_practice.prompt: A gardener picks 28 carrots and 15 radishes. How many vegetables is that?
guided_practice.hint: What do 8 + 5 make? Is that 10 or more? What do you do with the extra ten?

guided_practice.prompt: In the morning 46 beans are picked. In the afternoon 38 more are picked. How many beans altogether?
guided_practice.hint: Start with the ones: 6 + 8. Remember to regroup.

guided_practice.prompt: Work out 59 + 27 in columns. Ones: 9 + 7 = ___, so write ___ and carry ___ ten. Tens: 5 + 2 + 1 = ___.
guided_practice.hint: 9 + 7 = 16. Write the 6 and carry the 1 ten above the tens column.

guided_practice.prompt: A garden shop has 175 packets of seeds and gets 24 more. How many packets now?
guided_practice.hint: Keep the 100 aside. Add the tens, then the ones.
7 + 8 = 15, so you will regroup. Then add the tens, then bring the hundreds down.
guided_practice.answer: 305 (ones: 7 + 8 = 15, write 5 carry 1; tens: 6 + 3 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1; hundreds: 2 + 1 = 3).

guided_practice.prompt: Why do we regroup when the ones add up to 10 or more?
guided_practice.hint: How many ones make one ten?
options: Because 10 ones make 1 ten, and each place can only hold 0 to 9
Because the tens are bigger than the ones
Because we should always carry a number
guided_practice.answer: Because 10 ones make 1 ten, and each place can only hold 0 to 9

guided_practice.prompt: A school garden has 128 plants and plants 45 more. How many plants now?
guided_practice.hint: Add the ones first: 8 + 5. Then the tens: 2 tens + 4 tens + the regrouped ten.

activities.title: Bean cups: build it, add it, regroup it
activities.instructions: A hands-on way to see regrouping. Count out about 60 dried beans, buttons or pebbles and put exactly 10 in each small cup or bowl to make 'tens'. Show 27 as 2 full cups and 7 loose beans, and 18 as 1 full cup and 8 loose beans. Push them together and swap 10 loose beans for a new cup. Then answer the questions on screen to record what you found. (If you do not have beans, skip this activity; you will not miss any of the learning.)

tasks.prompt: Prediction: before you push 27 and 18 together, how many full cups and loose beans do you think you will have? Write your guess and why.
tasks.answer: A reasonable guess such as 3 cups and 15 loose beans, because 2 + 1 = 3 tens and 7 + 8 = 15 ones.

tasks.prompt: After regrouping, you have ___ full cups and ___ loose beans.
tasks.hint: Swap 10 of the 15 loose beans for another cup.

tasks.prompt: Now try 36 + 29 with your beans. What is the total?
tasks.answer: 65 (6 cups and 5 loose beans after regrouping).

tasks.prompt: Reflection: what did you notice when there were more than 10 loose beans? Explain in your own words.
tasks.answer: You swap 10 loose beans for 1 full cup (regroup), so the tens go up by one and the ones go down by ten.

activities.title: Plan a vegie patch
activities.instructions: A garden has three beds. Bed A has 34 plants, Bed B has 27 plants and Bed C has 19 plants. Work through the questions to find out how many plants the whole garden has.

tasks.prompt: Add Bed A and Bed B: 34 + 27.
tasks.hint: Add the tens, then the ones, then join them.

tasks.prompt: Now add Bed C to your answer: 61 + 19.
Which bed has the most plants?
Write a full sentence saying how many plants there are in the garden.
tasks.answer: There are 80 plants in the garden.

activities.title: Word match and column order
activities.instructions: Check that you know the language of adding and the steps of the column method.

tasks.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
tasks.answer: Tens/groups of ten; ones/single units; regroup/swap 10 ones for 1 ten; sum/total.

tasks.prompt: Put the steps of the column method in order.
options: Line up the digits in columns
Regroup if the ones make 10 or more
tasks.answer: Line up, add the ones, regroup if needed, add the tens, write the total.

tasks.prompt: A gardener has 48 tomato plants and plants 36 more. How many now?
Write your own garden story problem that needs regrouping, and solve it.
tasks.answer: Any problem with two two-digit numbers whose ones add to 10 or more, solved correctly.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what do you do when the ones add up to 13?
questions.answer_key: 13 ones is 1 ten and 3 ones. Write the 3 in the ones place and add the extra ten to the tens column (regroup or carry).

questions.prompt: A gardener has 148 daisies and 35 tulips. How many flowers does she have in total?
Work out 58 + 64 using the column method.
questions.answer_key: 122. Ones: 8 + 4 = 12, write 2 carry 1. Tens: 5 + 6 + 1 = 12, write 12. Answer 122.

questions.prompt: Sam says 45 + 28 = 613. What mistake did Sam make, and what is the correct answer?
questions.answer_key: Sam wrote 5 + 8 = 13 in the ones place without regrouping, and put 4 + 2 = 6 in front. The ones total 13 should be regrouped: write 3 and carry 1 ten. Tens: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. Correct answer 73.

quiz.question: You add the ones and get 14. What do you do?
options: Write 4 in the ones place and add 1 ten to the tens column
quiz.explanation: 14 ones is 1 ten and 4 ones, so the ten is regrouped into the tens column.

support: If your child finds regrouping hard: (1) stay with the bean cups until they can explain the trade of 10 loose beans for 1 cup without help; (2) use numbers where the ones just reach 10, such as 8 + 2, 6 + 4, before trying 8 + 7; (3) write each tens and ones step on a separate line; (4) use graph paper so digits line up in columns; (5) go back to examples without regrouping, like 24 + 35, and only add one new idea at a time.
extension: For a child who finishes early: (1) Add three numbers, such as 34 + 27 + 19, and explain the order you chose. (2) Invent a garden problem whose answer is exactly 100. (3) Find two numbers that have a 7 and a 6 in the ones place and add to a number between 80 and 90.
materials: About 60 dried beans, buttons or small pebbles
A real vegie patch or pot plants to count (optional)
parent_script:
Before you start: gather the beans and cups. Aim for about 60 minutes. Sit beside your child and keep the written work in front of them.

1. Hook (0 to 5 min): Read the introduction aloud. Ask: 'How could we find out how many seedlings there are without counting one by one?' Take a few guesses; do not correct yet.

2. Tens and ones (5 to 12 min): Read section 1 aloud. Make 47 with the bean cups (4 full cups and 7 loose). Ask your child to make 36. Ask: 'How many tens? How many ones?' Repeat with 52 and 29 until they answer without hesitation.

3. Add without regrouping (12 to 18 min): Read section 2. Work through worked example 1 together, writing each step on paper. Then ask them to explain in their own words why we add the tens and ones separately.

4. Regrouping (18 to 28 min): Read section 3. Build 47 and 36 with the beans, push them together, and let them discover there are 13 loose beans. Ask, 'What could we do with 10 of these?' Let them make the new cup. Then work through worked example 2. Common mistake: writing 13 in the ones column. Gently ask, 'How many digits can sit in the ones place?'

5. Column method (28 to 33 min): Read section 4 and show 47 + 36 in columns, lining digits up. Point at the carried 1 and say it is the new cup of ten.

6. Guided practice (33 to 43 min): Do guided practice questions 1 to 4 together. Child writes; you only give the hint if they are stuck for more than a minute. For questions 5 and 6 (bigger numbers) read section 5 first and do worked example 3.

7. Activities (43 to 53 min): Child does the bean cups activity and then plans the vegie patch. Walk away for a few minutes and check their working afterwards.

8. Check understanding (53 to 60 min): Child answers the written questions and then the quiz on screen. Use the answer key to mark. Celebrate correct reasoning, not just correct answers. If they get fewer than 3 of the 5 quiz questions, repeat the bean cups and section 3 tomorrow before moving on.
evidence_suggestions: A photo of the bean cups showing 27 + 18 regrouped into 4 cups and 5 loose beans.
The child's written working for the vegie patch plan (Bed A + Bed B + Bed C).
The child's own two garden story problems with solutions.
A short observation note: can the child explain what happens when the ones total 10 or more?

Guided practice: 1) 57  2) 43  3) 84  4) 86  5) 199  6) 305.
Activities: bean cups 27 + 18 = 45 and 36 + 29 = 65. Vegie patch: A + B = 34 + 27 = 61; 61 + C = 61 + 19 = 80, so 80 plants.
Questions: 1) 63  2) 13 ones = 1 ten and 3 ones; carry the ten  3) 183  4) 122  5) Sam forgot to regroup; the correct answer is 73.
Quiz: 1) 68  2) write 4 and add 1 ten to the tens column  3) 63  4) 156  5) 102.
offline_alternative: No screen needed for any part of this lesson except the final quiz. All the teaching, practice and activities can be done on paper with beans or buttons.
parent_notes: Reference example (not AI output) showing the depth a Side-Quest lesson should reach. Edit anything you like or delete it.
why_it_matters: Adding is one of the jobs you will do most in life: counting plants, money, distances, time. Quick, reliable addition with tens and ones is the foundation for every bigger calculation your child will meet, from multiplication to fractions. Understanding why regrouping works, not just how, is what stops children getting stuck later.
prior_knowledge: Can count to 100 and read two-digit numbers.
Knows that a two-digit number has a tens digit and a ones digit.
Can add single-digit numbers, such as 7 + 6, either from memory or by counting on.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing the whole 13 in the ones place, so 47 + 36 becomes 713 or 7 + 6 = 13 with nothing carried.
misconceptions.fix: Go back to the bean cups. Show that the ones place can only hold 9 loose beans before they must be packed into a cup of ten. Ask: 'How many loose beans can sit in the ones place?' Then regroup 13 into 1 ten and 3 ones before writing anything.

misconceptions.mistake: Forgetting to add the carried ten, so 47 + 36 comes out as 73.
misconceptions.fix: Point to the small 1 above the tens column and call it 'the new cup'. Tell your child to touch every digit in the tens column, including the small one, before writing the tens answer.

misconceptions.mistake: Lining digits up from the left instead of by place value, so 138 + 45 is written with the 4 under the 1.
misconceptions.fix: Draw ones, tens and hundreds boxes on the page and place one digit per box. Always start at the right-hand end of the number.

consolidation: Let's remember the three big ideas. First, every two-digit number is made of tens and ones, so 47 is 40 and 7. Second, we can add the tens and the ones separately and then join the answers. Third, when the ones add up to 10 or more, we regroup: 10 ones become 1 ten, and that ten joins the tens column. These ideas work for any size of number, whether you are counting seedlings or adding up a shop bill.

teaching_questions.ask: How many tens and how many ones are in 47?
Why do we add the tens separately from the ones?
teaching_questions.expected: Because tens and ones are different sized groups; we collect all the tens into one pile and all the ones into another and then join the piles.

teaching_questions.ask: What happens when the ones add up to more than 9?
teaching_questions.expected: We make a new ten out of 10 of the ones and move it into the tens column, leaving the extra ones behind.

teaching_questions.ask: How could you check that 47 + 36 = 83 is right?
teaching_questions.expected: Add in the other order (36 + 47), use bean cups, or estimate: 50 + 40 is about 90, so 83 is sensible.

teaching_questions.ask: What is the small 1 above the tens column in the column method?
teaching_questions.expected: It is the ten we made from 13 loose ones: the new cup.

teaching_plan: Concept: adding two-digit (and simple three-digit) numbers by working with tens and ones. Prior knowledge: place value of two-digit numbers and single-digit addition facts. Progression: (1) build numbers from tens and ones with beans; (2) add tens and ones separately when no regrouping is needed; (3) meet ones that total 10 or more and regroup them as a new ten; (4) record the same idea with the column method; (5) extend to a three-digit number plus a two-digit number. Likely misconceptions: writing 13 in the ones place, forgetting the carried ten, and lining digits up by the left edge. Assessment: written questions that mirror the worked examples, a spot-the-mistake question and a short quiz.

key_words.meaning: The single units in a number. In 47, the 7 is the ones.
Groups of ten. In 47, the 4 means 4 tens, which is 40.
To split a number into parts, like 47 = 40 + 7.
To swap 10 ones for 1 ten (or 10 tens for 1 hundred) when a place has 10 or more.
The answer when you add numbers together.
